claim: This study performs the first single-cell transcriptome analysis of cranial neural crest cell migration at three progressive stages in chick.
source: Here, we perform the first single-cell transcriptome analysis of cranial neural crest cell migration at three progressive stages in chick and identify and establish hierarchical relationships between cell position and time-specific transcriptional signatures.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this is the first single-cell transcriptome analysis of cranial neural crest cell migration at three progressive stages in chick.

claim: A novel transcriptional signature of the most invasive neural crest Trailblazer cells is enriched for approximately 900 genes.
source: We determine a novel transcriptional signature of the most invasive neural crest Trailblazer cells that is consistent during migration and enriched for approximately 900 genes.
evidence: The abstract states the Trailblazer signature is enriched for approximately 900 genes, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Knockdown of several Trailblazer genes shows significant but modest changes to total distance migrated.
source: Knockdown of several Trailblazer genes shows significant but modest changes to total distance migrated.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from knockdown experiments.

claim: In vivo expression analysis by RNAscope and immunohistochemistry reveals some salt and pepper patterns that include strong individual Trailblazer gene expression in cells within other subregions of the migratory stream.
source: However, in vivo expression analysis by RNAscope and immunohistochemistry reveals some salt and pepper patterns that include strong individual Trailblazer gene expression in cells within other subregions of the migratory stream.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this finding from RNAscope and immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: Neural crest cells undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition to exit the dorsal neural tube in a rostral-to-caudal timed manner.
source: Neural crest cells undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition to exit the dorsal neural tube in a rostral-to-caudal timed manner.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cranial neural crest cells travel in multicellular streams just underneath the surface ectoderm.
source: Cranial neural crest cells travel in multicellular streams just underneath the surface ectoderm, presenting the opportunity to visualize and interrogate the in vivo cellular and molecular features of the migration process.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cranial neural crest cell migration.

claim: The chick embryo is well suited to studying gene expression heterogeneities within neural crest cell migratory streams since cell isolation and single-cell RT-qPCR techniques have been optimized.
source: Furthermore, the chick embryo is well suited to studying gene expression heterogeneities within neural crest cell migratory streams since cell isolation and single-cell RT-qPCR techniques have been optimized (Morrison et al., 2012, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A unique molecular signature of 16 out of 96 genes was stable and consistent in a subset of cranial neural crest cells confined to the invasive front of the migratory stream termed 'trailblazers'.
source: Intriguingly, by optimizing a single-cell RT-qPCR method (Morrison et al., 2015), we were able to identify a unique molecular signature of 16 out of 96 genes that was stable and consistent in a subset of cranial neural crest cells confined to the invasive front of the migratory stream that we termed 'trailblazers' (McLennan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by McLennan et al., 2015.

claim: Over-expression of either of two transcription factors (TFAP2A, HAND2) upstream of the trailblazer genes in the follower cell subpopulation led to alterations in stream morphology.
source: Over-expression of either of two transcription factors (TFAP2A, HAND2) upstream of the trailblazer genes in the follower cell subpopulation led to alterations in stream morphology (McLennan et al., 2015) suggesting a functional role for trailblazer genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by McLennan et al., 2015.

claim: 469 cells were collected from the front, lead, and trail subregions of a typical cranial neural crest cell migratory stream at three developmental stages.
source: To do this, we compare gene expression fingerprints from 469 cells collected from the front, lead, and trail subregions of a typical cranial neural crest cell migratory stream at three developmental stages corresponding to initiation of migration from the dorsal neural tube, active migration towards and colonization of the branchial arches.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the number of cells analyzed.

claim: Approximately 100 migrating neural crest cells were collected from explanted cranial neural tube cultures for comparison to in vivo transcriptional signatures.
source: We additionally profiled ~100 migrating neural crest cells collected from explanted cranial neural tube cultures for comparison to in vivo transcriptional signatures.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the number of in vitro cells analyzed.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq was performed on cranial neural crest cells isolated from the invasive front and remainder of the migratory stream at HHSt13 and HHSt15.
source: To do this, we first performed bulk RNA-seq on cranial neural crest cells isolated from the invasive front and remainder of the migratory stream at two successive developmental stages during migration and branchial arch entry (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Hamburger and Hamilton, 1951, HHSt13 and HHSt15).
evidence: The results section describes the bulk RNA-seq experiment with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: At HHSt13 and HHSt15, chick cranial neural crest cells of the pre-otic stream adjacent to rhombomere 4 (r4) are mid-migration and colonizing the branchial arch targets, respectively.
source: At these successive developmental stages, chick cranial neural crest cells of the pre-otic stream adjacent to rhombomere 4 (r4) are mid-migration and colonizing the branchial arch targets, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the developmental stages analyzed in the study.

claim: Premigratory neural crest cells were fluorescently labeled with Gap43-YFP at HHSt8-9.
source: We fluorescently labeled premigratory neural crest cells with Gap43-YFP (at HHSt8-9; 4–7 somites), reincubated eggs until HHSt13 or HHSt15 and carefully manually dissected cells from the migratory front (5% of the stream, termed 'Front') and remainder of the stream (95% of the stream, termed 'Stream') (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for cell labeling.

claim: Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) was used to isolate neural crest cells from manually dissected tissues to perform bulk RNA-seq.
source: We then used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate neural crest cells from manually dissected tissues to perform bulk RNA-seq.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for cell isolation.

claim: Hierarchical clustering showed good correlation of expression levels between the three biological replicates in bulk RNA-seq.
source: Hierarchical clustering showed three distinct features of the data (Figure 1B). First, we find good correlation of expression levels between the three biological replicates, validating our cells isolations (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows the hierarchical clustering results validating the experimental approach.

claim: There are statistically significant differences in the expression levels of subsets of genes between the different subpopulations isolated in bulk RNA-seq.
source: Second, there are statistically significant differences in the expression levels of subsets of genes between the different subpopulations isolated, confirming a conserved invasion signature within the front migrating cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 1B and source data show statistically significant differences between subpopulations.

claim: Subsets of genes expressed in the front subpopulation were either consistently up- or down-regulated in comparison to the remainder of the stream at both developmental stages.
source: Third, subsets of genes expressed in the front subpopulation were either consistently up- or down-regulated in comparison to the remainder of the stream at both developmental stages (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 1B shows consistent up- or down-regulation of gene subsets.

claim: There is a subset of 23 genes enriched in some neural crest cells at the invasive front compared with the remainder of the stream, with consistent expression at both HHSt13 and HHSt15.
source: We find there is a subset of genes enriched in some neural crest cells at the invasive front compared with the remainder of the stream, with consistent expression at both developmental stages and unique to the previous 16 gene scRT-qPCR signature (Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1; n = 23 genes).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the Venn diagram with 23 genes enriched at both stages.

claim: There is a subset of 19 genes reduced in migrating front cells compared with the remainder of the stream, with consistent expression at both HHSt13 and HHSt15.
source: In contrast, we find a subset of genes reduced in migrating front cells compared with the remainder of the stream, with consistent expression at both developmental stages (Figure 1E; m = 19 genes).
evidence: Figure 1E shows the Venn diagram with 19 genes reduced at both stages.

claim: Bulk RNA-seq analysis validated that ITGB5 and GPC3 (HHSt13), and BAMBI and PKP2 (HHSt15) were enriched in FRONT versus stream samples.
source: In comparison to our previous identification of 16 genes out of 100 analyzed by scRT-qPCR (McLennan et al., 2015), bulk RNA-seq analysis validated that ITGB5 and GPC3 (HHSt13), and BAMBI and PKP2 (HHSt15) were enriched in FRONT versus stream samples.
evidence: This compares bulk RNA-seq results to previous RT-qPCR findings.

claim: EPHA4 (HHSt13) and CDH7 (HHSt15) were reduced in FRONT versus stream samples.
source: EPHA4 (HHSt13) and CDH7 (HHSt15) were reduced.
evidence: This describes genes reduced in the front subpopulation.

claim: Individual cells were isolated from different stream positions at three developmental stages (HHSt11, 13, 15) for single-cell RNA-seq.
source: To better characterize unique transcriptional signatures and gene expression heterogeneity during cranial neural crest migration, we isolated and profiled individual cells from different stream positions at three developmental stages (HHSt11,13,15; Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for single-cell RNA-seq.

claim: The three progressive developmental stages (HHSt11, 13, 15) were selected based on different migratory events including recently delaminated from the neural tube, invasion of the paraxial mesoderm, and entry into the second branchial arch with approximately 8 hr in between the stages.
source: These three progressive developmental stages were selected based on the different migratory events including recently delaminated from the neural tube (HHSt11), invasion of the paraxial mesoderm (HHSt13) and entry into the second branchial arch (HHSt15) with ~8 hr in between the stages.
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting these specific developmental stages.

claim: Neural crest cell migratory streams at HHSt13 and HHSt15 were subdivided into three spatially distinct, non-overlapping subregions: Front (5% of the stream), Lead (25% of the stream), and Trail (70% of the stream).
source: This included neural crest cells within the invasive front (5% of the stream, termed 'Front'), lead subregion of the stream (25% of the stream just proximal to the front, termed 'Lead'), and remainder of the stream (70% of the stream, termed 'Trail') (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes how the migratory stream was subdivided for analysis.

claim: At HHSt11, the stream was not subdivided since there are relatively small numbers of migrating neural crest cells adjacent to rhombomere 4 (r4).
source: At HHSt11, we did not subdivide the stream since there are relatively small numbers of migrating neural crest cells adjacent to rhombomere 4 (r4) and refer to these cells as 'Front' (Figure 2A).
evidence: This explains why HHSt11 cells were not subdivided.

claim: The total number of single cells analyzed after quality control was 469.
source: The total number of single cells analyzed after quality control was 469 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows the number of single cells analyzed.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of single neural crest cell averages revealed statistically enriched and reduced genes between every pairwise combination of subpopulations.
source: Hierarchical clustering of single neural crest cell averages revealed statistically enriched and reduced genes between every pairwise combination of subpopulations and concordance between Lead cells at HHSt13 and HHSt15 and Trail cells at HHSt13 and HHSt15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows the hierarchical clustering results.

claim: Spatial location within the stream and temporal progression along the migratory pathway are primary determinants of gene expression.
source: These data show that spatial location within the stream and temporal progression along the migratory pathway are primary determinants of gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: The average in vitro profile is prominently distinct from all in vivo profiles analyzed.
source: First, using a Pearson correlation matrix to relate the average expression profile of all migrating neural crest cell subpopulations to show that the average in vitro profile is prominently distinct from all in vivo profiles analyzed (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows the Pearson correlation matrix demonstrating this distinction.

claim: The in vitro neural crest cell gene expression profile correlates most closely with cells most recently exited from the dorsal neural tube (HHSt11).
source: Specifically, the in vitro neural crest cell gene expression profile correlates poorly with every isolated in vivo subpopulation. The closest correlation is cells most recently exited from the dorsal neural tube (HHSt11) (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 2C shows the correlation between in vitro and HHSt11 cells.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) reveals that all in vitro single neural crest cells cluster together and show minimal overlap with any in vivo single-cell expression profile.
source: The PCA reveals that all in vitro single neural crest cells cluster together and show minimal overlap with any in vivo single-cell expression profile (Figure 2D).
evidence: Figure 2D shows the PCA plot demonstrating this clustering.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) Term analysis shows enrichment of genes associated with biological processes such as cell signaling, transcription regulation, growth factor response, migration and proliferation by in vivo neural crest cells when compared to in vitro data.
source: From this analysis, there is enrichment of genes associated with biological processes such as cell signaling, transcription regulation, growth factor response, migration and proliferation by in vivo neural crest cells when compared to in vitro data (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows the GO term analysis results.

claim: 806 genes are down-regulated in neural crest cells grown in vitro compared with in vivo data.
source: We find that 806 genes are down-regulated in neural crest cells grown in vitro (e.g., NKX2-5, NKX2-6, WNT5B, SNAI1, PAX5, PAX9, HAND1, PHOX2B, EPHA3, EPHA5, NCAM2, FGFs 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 18, 19, AQPs 1, 3, 5, NEUROD1, NGFR, NRP1, DLXs 1, 3, 5, 6, TWIST1, TGFBR2, DSP, CDHs 5, 10, CXCL12, GATA4, GATA6, GPC3, ISL1, BMP2, and KDR (VEGFR2)) compared with in vivo data (Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Figure 2F shows examples of genes down-regulated in vitro.

claim: 312 genes are up-regulated in migrating neural crest cells in vitro compared with in vivo data.
source: We also find 312 genes up-regulated in migrating neural crest cells in vitro (e.g., WNT9A, SHH, SOX2, PAX7, IL8, MKX, CDH6 and CDH12) (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This describes genes up-regulated in vitro.

claim: Despite the identification of 312 genes up-regulated in migrating neural crest cells in vitro, no GO terms were associated with these genes.
source: However, despite the identification of 312 genes up-regulated in migrating neural crest cells in vitro, we did not find any GO terms associated with these genes.
evidence: This describes the lack of GO term enrichment for up-regulated in vitro genes.

claim: In vivo embryonic neural crest cell microenvironmental signals influence both the spatial and temporal heterogeneities of neural crest cell gene expression and biological processes critical to migration and embryogenesis.
source: These data strongly suggest that in vivo embryonic neural crest cell microenvironmental signals influence both the spatial and temporal heterogeneities of neural crest cell gene expression and biological processes critical to migration and embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Hierarchical clustering identifies subsets of genes that either increased or decreased with developmental stage and spatial location within the stream.
source: Second, we identify subsets of genes that either increased (Figure 3, box A) or decreased (Figure 3, box B) with developmental stage and spatial location within the stream.
evidence: Figure 3 shows the heatmap with boxes A and B highlighting these gene subsets.

claim: Subsets of genes were uniquely reduced or enhanced in individual subpopulations of migrating neural crest cells.
source: Third, we discover subsets of genes that were uniquely reduced (Figure 3, box A') or enhanced (Figure 3, box C) in individual subpopulations of migrating neural crest cells.
evidence: Figure 3 shows boxes A' and C highlighting these unique gene subsets.

claim: Some genes show expression changes that correlate with spatial position within the stream at a single developmental time point.
source: Fourth, we find that some genes show expression changes that correlate with spatial position within the stream at a single developmental time point (Figure 3, box D).
evidence: Figure 3 shows box D highlighting these spatially correlated genes.

claim: Heterogeneity of expression among single cells within any subpopulation was common.
source: Lastly, we identify that heterogeneity of expression among single cells within any subpopulation was common (Figure 3).
evidence: Figure 3 shows the heterogeneity of expression within subpopulations.

claim: A Pearson correlation matrix of all single-cell transcriptomes confirmed similarity among some, but not all cells within each subpopulation.
source: A Pearson correlation matrix of all single-cell transcriptomes confirmed similarity among some, but not all cells within each subpopulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that our spatial-temporal locations are not completely homogeneous.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the Pearson correlation matrix.

claim: Each cranial neural crest cell subpopulation analyzed (Front, Lead, Trail) can be defined by distinct molecular signatures, but also include heterogeneity of expression.
source: These results demonstrate that each cranial neural crest cell subpopulation analyzed (Front, Lead, Trail) can be defined by distinct molecular signatures, but also include heterogeneity of expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of single-cell transcriptomes.

claim: Hierarchical clustering reveals that the majority of neural crest cells at the invasive front cluster together by developmental stage.
source: First, hierarchical clustering reveals that the majority of neural crest cells at the invasive front cluster together by developmental stage (Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 4A shows the hierarchical clustering of invasive front cells.

claim: A Pearson correlation matrix shows that neural crest cells within the invasive front at HHSt13 and HHSt15 have expression profiles that cluster most similarly with Lead cell subpopulations, termed Lead-like.
source: Further, a Pearson correlation matrix shows that neural crest cells within the invasive front at HHSt13 and HHSt15 have expression profiles that cluster most similarly with Lead cell subpopulations, which we termed Lead-like (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows the Pearson correlation matrix identifying Lead-like cells.

claim: Two distinct cell subpopulations exist at HHSt11 termed Cluster1 and Cluster2.
source: Second, we discover two distinct cell subpopulations exist at HHSt11 termed Cluster1 and Cluster2 (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Figure 4A-B shows the two distinct clusters at HHSt11.

claim: A distinct cluster contains neural crest cells isolated from the invasive front at all three developmental stages analyzed, termed scRNA-seq Trailblazers.
source: Third, we find a distinct cluster that contains neural crest cells isolated from the invasive front at all three developmental stages analyzed, termed scRNA-seq Trailblazers (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows the Trailblazer cluster.

claim: The single-cell PCA plot shows five distinct cell subpopulations within the invasive front over time, with very minimal overlap in expression profile between the Trailblazer cluster and any other cell subpopulation cluster.
source: The single-cell PCA plot shows these five distinct cell subpopulations within the invasive front over time, with very minimal overlap in expression profile between the Trailblazer cluster and any other cell subpopulation cluster (Figure 4C; light blue dots).
evidence: Figure 4C shows the PCA plot with five distinct subpopulations.

claim: The identification of a transcriptomic signature associated with Trailblazer cells within the invasive front represents an unbiased and more comprehensive molecular profile than previously described by scRT-qPCR.
source: The identification of a transcriptomic signature associated with Trailblazer cells within the invasive front represents an unbiased and more comprehensive molecular profile than we previously described by scRT-qPCR (McLennan et al., 2015).
evidence: This compares the current scRNA-seq results to previous RT-qPCR findings.

claim: 964 genes are up-regulated in Trailblazers.
source: A volcano plot shows that 964 genes are up-regulated (e.g., BAMBI, LUM, MMP2, GATA2, GATA4, GATA5 and GATA6) and 406 genes are down-regulated (e.g., DRAXIN, TFAP2A, TFAP2B, TFAP2C, TFAP2E and SOX10) within the Trailblazers (Figure 5A and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 5A shows the volcano plot with up-regulated genes in Trailblazers.

claim: 406 genes are down-regulated in Trailblazers.
source: A volcano plot shows that 964 genes are up-regulated (e.g., BAMBI, LUM, MMP2, GATA2, GATA4, GATA5 and GATA6) and 406 genes are down-regulated (e.g., DRAXIN, TFAP2A, TFAP2B, TFAP2C, TFAP2E and SOX10) within the Trailblazers (Figure 5A and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 5A shows the volcano plot with down-regulated genes in Trailblazers.

claim: Nineteen out of 24 genes (79%) enriched in the invasive front from bulk RNA-seq analysis were also enriched in Trailblazers by scRNA-seq.
source: Nineteen out of 24 genes (79%) enriched in the invasive front from our bulk RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1D) were also enriched in Trailblazers by scRNA-seq (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This compares bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq results.

claim: 7 out of 19 genes (37%) reduced in the invasive front from bulk RNA-seq analysis were also reduced in Trailblazers by scRNA-seq.
source: Additionally, 7 out of 19 genes (37%) reduced in the invasive front from our bulk RNA-seq analysis (Figure 1E) were also reduced in Trailblazers by scRNA-seq (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This compares bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq results.

claim: Known neural crest-related genes that are up-regulated in Trailblazers include EDN1, GPC3, NRP1, BMP2, AQP1, BAMBI, and PKP2.
source: We also find examples of known neural crest-related genes that are up-regulated in Trailblazers (e.g., EDN1, GPC3, NRP1, BMP2) and include genes (AQP1, BAMBI, PKP2) identified in our RT-qPCR analysis (McLennan et al., 2015) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows examples of up-regulated neural crest-related genes in Trailblazers.

claim: Neural crest-related genes down-regulated in Trailblazers include MSX1, EDNRB, PAX3, and SOX10.
source: There are also neural crest-related genes down-regulated in Trailblazers (e.g., MSX1, EDNRB, PAX3, SOX10) (Figure 5B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 5B shows examples of down-regulated neural crest-related genes in Trailblazers.

claim: At HHSt11, approximately 8% of the migrating neural crest cells had a Trailblazer transcriptional signature.
source: At HHSt11 we found that approximately 8% of the migrating neural crest cells had a Trailblazer transcriptional signature.
evidence: This describes the proportion of Trailblazer cells at HHSt11.

claim: By HHSt13, 49% of the cells within the invasive front had a Trailblazer transcriptional signature, or around 12 cells.
source: By HHSt13, with an estimate of approximately 500 neural crest cells in the typical migratory stream at this stage and axial level, we found that 49% of the cells within the invasive front had a Trailblazer transcriptional signature, or around 12 cells.
evidence: This describes the proportion and number of Trailblazer cells at HHSt13.

claim: At HHSt15, approximately 32% (or around 13 cells within the invasive front of a stream of approximately 800 cells) had a Trailblazer transcriptional signature.
source: At HHSt15, approximately 32% (or around 13 cells within the invasive front of a stream of approximately 800 cells) had a Trailblazer transcriptional signature.
evidence: This describes the proportion and number of Trailblazer cells at HHSt15.

claim: Fewer than 10% of neural crest cells in other subregions of the migratory stream show expression profiles that overlap with any of the Trailblazer cells.
source: We find that fewer than 10% of neural crest cells in other subregions of the migratory stream show expression profiles that overlap with any of the Trailblazer cells (Figure 5C; Lead (n = 8 out of 100 cells) and Trail (m = 10 out of 110 cells)).
evidence: Figure 5C shows the PCA plot demonstrating minimal overlap.

claim: Neural crest cells with a Trailblazer transcriptional signature are mostly confined to the invasive front of the migratory stream.
source: These data suggest that neural crest cells with a Trailblazer transcriptional signature are mostly confined to the invasive front of the migratory stream.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PCA analysis.

claim: Of the genes differentially expressed by Trailblazers and classified into known pathways, 81% were increased and only 19% were decreased.
source: We find that of the genes differentially expressed by Trailblazers and classified into known pathways, 81% were increased and only 19% were decreased (Figure 5D; red and blue numbers respectively).
evidence: Figure 5D shows the pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Increased genes in Trailblazers are associated with pathways such as WNT/Beta Catenin, tight junction, Rho-family GTPases, EMT, integrin, gap junction, endothelin-1 and BMP signaling.
source: We find increased genes associated with pathways such as WNT/Beta Catenin, tight junction, Rho-family GTPases, EMT, integrin, gap junction, endothelin-1 and BMP signaling (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows the pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: Trailblazers show increased expression of VEGF receptors 1, 2 and 3 as well as neuropilin-1 (NRP1).
source: Consistent with our previous findings that VEGF/neuropilin-1 chemoattraction guides cranial neural crest cell migration (McLennan and Kulesa, 2007; McLennan et al., 2010; McLennan and Kulesa, 2010; McLennan et al., 2015), we find that increased expression of VEGF receptors 1, 2 and 3 as well as neuropilin-1 (NRP1) in the Trailblazers (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows increased VEGF signaling genes in Trailblazers, consistent with previous findings.

claim: 37 genes associated with axonal guidance signaling are expressed at significantly higher levels by the Trailblazers, including members of the BMP, EPH, MMP and WNT families.
source: Further, 37 genes associated with axonal guidance signaling are expressed at significantly higher levels by the Trailblazers, including members of the BMP, EPH, MMP and WNT families (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows the axonal guidance signaling genes enriched in Trailblazers.

claim: Four genes (AQP1, BAMBI, CTNNB1 and PKP2) from the 16 gene RT-qPCR Trailblazer signature were enriched in both RT-qPCR and scRNA-seq analyses.
source: When we examined the presence of our 16 gene RT-qPCR Trailblazer signature (McLennan et al., 2015) within the scRNA-seq data, we found four genes (AQP1, BAMBI, CTNNB1 and PKP2) enriched in both analyses (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E compares the RT-qPCR and scRNA-seq Trailblazer signatures.

claim: The HHSt15 Lead-like subpopulation showed an increase of ITGB5 and NEDD9.
source: The HHSt15 Lead-like subpopulation that was included in our RT-qPCR Trailblazer subpopulation (defined by manual dissection and not molecular signature) showed an increase of ITGB5 and NEDD9 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows genes enriched in the Lead-like subpopulation.

claim: EPHB1 was enriched in HHSt11 Cluster1 compared to all other migrating cells profiled from in vivo.
source: Of the other 16 genes, EPHB1 was enriched in HHSt11 Cluster1 compared to all other migrating cells profiled from in vivo (Figure 5E) and CDH7 and CXCR4 were enriched in HHSt11 Cluster2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows genes enriched in HHSt11 Cluster1.

claim: CDH7 and CXCR4 were enriched in HHSt11 Cluster2.
source: Of the other 16 genes, EPHB1 was enriched in HHSt11 Cluster1 compared to all other migrating cells profiled from in vivo (Figure 5E) and CDH7 and CXCR4 were enriched in HHSt11 Cluster2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows genes enriched in HHSt11 Cluster2.

claim: Differential expression analysis between HHSt11 Cluster1 and Cluster2 showed that CDH11, CXCR4, NEDD9, TFAP2A and TFAP2B were enriched in HHSt11 Cluster2 compared to Cluster1.
source: Differential expression analysis between HHSt11 Cluster1 and Cluster2 showed that CDH11, CXCR4, NEDD9, and TFAP2A and TFAP2B were enriched in HHSt11 Cluster2 compared to Cluster1, but no gene of the 16 RT-qPCR signature genes were enriched in HHSt11 Cluster1 versus Cluster2 (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This describes differential expression between HHSt11 clusters.

claim: None of the 13 genes tested by RNAscope are expressed in all of, or the majority of cells at the invasive front.
source: We find that none of the 13 genes tested are expressed in all of, or the majority of cells at the invasive front (Figure 6A–M).
evidence: Figure 6A-M shows RNAscope expression patterns for 13 genes.

claim: Some genes appear expressed in a few or some but not in all of the cells (~30%) of the (narrow) front migratory edge.
source: That is, some genes appear expressed in a few or some but not in all of the cells (~30%) of the (narrow) front migratory edge (Figure 6A–M).
evidence: Figure 6A-M shows heterogeneous expression at the front.

claim: Plakophilin2 (PKP2) and Kazal Type Serine Peptidase Inhibitor Domain 1 (KAZALD1) showed heterogeneity of expression between invasive front neighboring cells.
source: For example, Plakophilin2 (PKP2) and Kazal Type Serine Peptidase Inhibitor Domain 1 (KAZALD1) showed heterogeneity of expression between invasive front neighboring cells (Figure 6A–A", C–C"; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Figure 6A-A" and C-C" show heterogeneous expression of PKP2 and KAZALD1.

claim: Some of the 13 genes analyzed by RNAscope display salt and pepper patterns that include strong expression in a few cells in the invasive front and similarly strong signal in some cells in the beginning or middle portions of the stream.
source: Further, some of the 13 genes analyzed by RNAscope display salt and pepper patterns that include strong expression in a few cells in the invasive front and similarly strong signal in some cells in the beginning or middle portions of the stream (not at the front edge of migration).
evidence: This describes salt and pepper expression patterns observed by RNAscope.

claim: Desmin (DES) and Tescalcin (TESC) are expressed within the invasive front and also in migrating neural crest cells within the remainder of the stream.
source: We found Desmin (DES) and Tescalcin (TESC) to be expressed within the invasive front (Figure B,D; green shading), but also in migrating neural crest cells within the remainder of the stream (Figure 6B,D; red sharing).
evidence: Figure 6B and D show expression of DES and TESC in both front and stream.

claim: TroponinI1 Slow Skeletal Type (TNNI1), Glypican3, and TFPI2 showed strong signal in some cells in the middle or back portions of the stream.
source: Lastly, some of the 13 genes were not found at the invasive front, and instead appear to be expressed more strongly at various positions within the migratory stream. That is, TroponinI1 Slow Skeletal Type (TNNI1), Glypican3, and TFPI2 showed strong signal in some cells in the middle or back portions of the stream (Figure 6E,G,L).
evidence: Figure 6E, G, and L show expression of TNNI1, Glypican3, and TFPI2 in the middle or back of the stream.

claim: Knockdown of WNT5B led to a 21% reduction in neural crest cell distance migrated (p=0.0001).
source: Specifically, we found that WNT5B showed the most significant change in neural crest cell migration (21% reduction in distance migrated) (Figure 6P,Q).
evidence: Figure 6P and Q show the effect of WNT5B knockdown on migration distance.

claim: Knockdown of PKP2 led to a significant reduction (13%) in neural crest cell distance migrated (p=0.017).
source: We found that knockdown of 3 of these genes (WNT5B (p=0.0001), PKP2 (p=0.017), EDN1 (p=0.004)) led to a significant reduction (>13%) in neural crest cell distance migrated (Figure 6N–Q).
